stem: Which soil type drains fastest after heavy rain?

options.content: Sandy soil
options.rationale: Correct: large pores let water drain quickly.

options.content: Clay soil
options.rationale: Clay has tiny pores and drains slowly.

options.content: Loam soil
options.rationale: Loam drains well, but more slowly than sand.

options.content: Silty clay soil
options.rationale: Fine particles make it drain slowly.

explanation: Sand particles are large, so the pores between them are large and water drains through fast.

stem: Why do clay soils hold more plant nutrients than sandy soils?

options.content: Clay particles have a very large surface area that holds nutrients
options.rationale: Correct: nutrients are held on the surfaces of the tiny clay particles.

options.content: Clay particles are larger, so they contain more minerals
options.rationale: Clay particles are the smallest soil particles.

options.content: Clay soils drain fast, so fertiliser reaches the roots very quickly after rain
options.rationale: Clay drains slowly; fast drainage causes leaching.

options.content: Clay soils are warmer, so nutrients dissolve faster
options.rationale: Clay soils warm slowly.

explanation: Many tiny clay particles give a huge total surface area that holds nutrient ions against leaching. Sandy soils have a small surface area, so nutrients leach easily.

stem: Farmers call clay soils "heavy" because they

options.content: weigh more per bucket than any other soil when dry
options.rationale: The term is about workability, not mass.

options.content: contain heavy gravel and stones
options.rationale: Clay soils have the finest particles.

options.content: sink below sandy soils in the soil profile
options.rationale: Soil types do not sink below one another.

options.content: need much effort to cultivate: sticky when wet and hard when dry
options.rationale: Correct: 'heavy' refers to how hard they are to work.

explanation: Heavy and light describe workability: clay is sticky when wet and hard when dry; sand is easy to work.

stem: Which soil warms up most quickly at the start of the rainy season?

options.content: Clay soil
options.rationale: Clay holds much water, which needs a lot of heat to warm.

options.content: Waterlogged loam
options.rationale: Waterlogged soil warms slowly.

options.content: Silty clay soil
options.rationale: Fine, water-holding soils warm slowly.

options.content: Sandy soil
options.rationale: Correct: it holds little water and has large air spaces, so it heats quickly.

explanation: Water needs a lot of energy to warm up. Sandy soils hold little water, so they warm quickly; wet clay soils warm slowly.

stem: In a capillary experiment, water eventually rises highest in a clay soil. What is the best explanation?

options.content: Clay particles are larger than sand grains, so each one lifts more water upwards
options.rationale: Clay particles are the smallest particles.

options.content: The pores between clay particles are very narrow, so they act as fine capillary tubes
options.rationale: Correct: the narrower the pore, the higher water rises by capillarity.

options.content: Clay contains more air, which pushes water upwards
options.rationale: Air does not drive capillary rise.

options.content: Clay drains fastest of all soils, so water moves through it quickly in every direction
options.rationale: Clay drains slowly; capillary rise in clay is slow but high.

explanation: Capillary rise is greatest in the narrowest pores. Clay's tiny pores lift water highest, though slowly; sand's large pores give a fast but low rise.
hints: Think about water rising in a very thin glass tube.

stem: Sipho wants to improve the water-holding capacity of the sandy soil in his vegetable garden. Which action would help most?

options.content: Ploughing the garden more often to loosen the sand
options.rationale: More tillage oxidises organic matter and does not hold water.

options.content: Adding more sand from a riverbed to the beds
options.rationale: More sand makes drainage even faster.

options.content: Burning grass on the beds before planting
options.rationale: Burning destroys organic matter.

options.content: Digging in well-rotted manure or compost every season
options.rationale: Correct: humus holds water and binds sand into crumbs.

explanation: Organic matter (humus) holds several times its own mass of water and improves crumb structure. Mulch and anthill soil also help.
hints: Which soil component absorbs water like a sponge?

stem: A clay field near Gweru is acid, waterlogged after storms and forms large clods when ploughed. Which plan would best improve it?

options.content: Add sand, burn the residues and plough when the soil is wet
options.rationale: Burning removes organic matter and ploughing wet soil smears it.

options.content: Irrigate heavily, then plough deeper every year, always at the same depth
options.rationale: More water worsens waterlogging; same-depth ploughing forms pans.

options.content: Apply lime, add manure, plant on ridges and plough only when moist
options.rationale: Correct: lime and humus improve structure, ridges improve drainage and timing avoids clods.

options.content: Apply only nitrogen fertiliser and leave the field bare
options.rationale: Fertiliser alone does not improve structure or drainage.

explanation: Calcium from lime flocculates clay and corrects acidity; organic matter opens the soil into crumbs; ridges or drains remove excess water; working at the right moisture avoids clods.
hints: Address acidity, structure, drainage and the timing of tillage.

stem: Loam is usually the best soil for most crops because it combines good drainage with good water-holding and fertility.
explanation: True. Loam has a balanced mixture of sand, silt and clay with humus, giving a mix of large and small pores.

stem: Because clay soils hold the most water, all of that water is available to crops.
explanation: False. Some water in clay is held so tightly in tiny pores and on particle surfaces that roots cannot take it up. Available water is often greatest in loams.
hints: Think about how tightly tiny pores hold water.

stem: Match each property with the soil type it best describes.

left.content: Balanced mixture with humus; easy to work and fertile

explanation: Sandy soils leach; clay soils crack when dry and waterlog when wet; loams are balanced and fertile.

payload.template: Sandy soils have {{blank:a}} pores and {{blank:b}} water-holding capacity. Clay soils warm up {{blank:c}} in spring.

explanation: Sand: large pores, low water holding. Clay: holds much water, so it warms slowly.

stem: Tatenda pours 150 mL of water onto a dry soil in a funnel. After 30 minutes 96 mL has drained into the cylinder. How much water, in mL, did the soil retain?
explanation: Water retained = water poured − water collected = 150 − 96 = 54 mL. 96 mL is the water that drained, not the water held.
workedSolution: 1. Water retained = water poured − water collected = 150 − 96 = 54 mL. 96 mL is the water that drained, not the water held.

stem: Name the soil type that is a balanced mixture of sand, silt and clay with a good humus content.
explanation: A **loam** combines the good properties of sand and clay.

stem: Name a material that is rich in clay and is often mixed into sandy garden soil in Zimbabwe to improve its water-holding.
explanation: **Anthill (termite-mound) soil** is finer and richer in clay than the surrounding sand.

stem: Compare sandy and clay soils in terms of drainage and aeration. Explain each difference.

points.description: Sandy soil drains quickly whereas clay soil drains slowly.
Because sand has large pores, clay tiny pores that hold water.
Sandy soil is well aerated whereas clay soil is poorly aerated when wet.
Because clay's tiny pores stay full of water, leaving little room for air.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Sandy soil drains quickly whereas clay drains slowly, because sand has large pores and clay has tiny pores that hold water. Sandy soil is well aerated whereas clay is poorly aerated when wet, because its small pores stay filled with water.

explanation: Compare with matched statements and explain using particle and pore size.
hints: Link each property to pore size.

stem:
Three soils, X, Y and Z, were tested. Equal masses of each dry soil were placed in funnels, and 250 mL of water was poured onto each at the same time.

| Soil | Water poured (mL) | Water collected after 20 min (mL) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| X | 250 | 185 |
| Y | 250 | 140 |
| Z | 250 | 90 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the volume of water retained by soil Z, in mL.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Express the water retained by soil Z as a percentage of the water poured.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Which soil is most likely to be the sandy soil?

options.content: Y
options.rationale: Y retained more than X, so it has finer particles.

options.content: X
options.rationale: Correct: most water drained through it in 20 minutes.

options.content: Z
options.rationale: Z retained the most water: it is the most clayey.

options.content: Y and Z equally
options.rationale: They gave very different results.

parts.explanation: The sandy soil has the largest pores, so the most water drains through it.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: State **two** variables, other than those in the stem, that should be kept the same to make the test fair.

points.description: Same size of funnel / same amount of cotton wool in each.
Same time allowed for drainage / same dryness of soil at the start / soil not compacted differently.

parts.explanation: Only the soil type should change.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Suggest which soil would need irrigation most often in a dry spell, and explain why.

points.description: It retains the least water, so the crop uses up the stored water soonest.

parts.explanation: Low water-holding capacity means short intervals between irrigations.

explanation: A drainage test compares water-holding: retained = poured − collected, and the least-draining soil has the finest particles.
hints: The soil that collects least water holds most.

stem:
Glass tubes filled with three soils, A, B and C, were stood in a tray of water. The height of wet soil was measured.

| Time | Soil A (cm) | Soil B (cm) | Soil C (cm) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 10 minutes | 6 | 4 | 2 |
| 1 hour | 11 | 10 | 6 |
| 1 day | 16 | 24 | 31 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: By how many cm did the water in soil C rise between 1 hour and 1 day?

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which soil is most likely to be the clay soil?

options.content: Soil A
options.rationale: A rose fastest at first but least overall: sand.

options.content: Soil B
options.rationale: B is intermediate: probably loam.

options.content: Soil C
options.rationale: Correct: slow at first but the highest rise, typical of tiny pores.

options.content: None, because clay does not allow capillary rise
options.rationale: Clay gives the highest capillary rise.

parts.explanation: Clay pores are narrowest, giving the highest but slowest capillary rise.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain the results for soil A, and suggest why this soil type dries out quickly at the surface in the dry season.

points.description: Soil A (sand) has large pores, so water rises quickly at first.
But large pores cannot hold water high against gravity, so the final rise is low.
Little water moves up from deeper layers to replace water evaporated at the surface.
And sand holds little water anyway, so the surface dries quickly.

parts.explanation: Large pores: fast, low capillary rise and little resupply to the surface.

explanation: Narrow pores give high capillary rise; wide pores give a fast but low rise.
hints: Which soil started fastest and which went highest?

stem: A school has a choice of two sites for a vegetable garden: a sandy site close to a borehole, or a clay site 400 m from the nearest water. Discuss which site is better.

points.description: Sandy site: easy to work, warms quickly, good drainage and aeration for vegetables.
But low water and nutrient holding: needs frequent watering and regular manure/fertiliser.
Water is close, so frequent watering is practical; manure and mulch can improve the sand.
Clay site: holds water and nutrients well.
But heavy to work, may waterlog, and carrying water 400 m is difficult in the dry season.
Judgement with reason, e.g. the sandy site is better because its weaknesses can be managed and water is available.

levels.descriptor: Accurate, well-developed explanation of several relevant points using correct agricultural terms, applied to the crop, animal or situation in the question, with a clear judgement where one is asked for.
Some relevant points explained, partly developed or only partly applied to the situation; any judgement is simple or one-sided.
Simple statements or a list of points with little explanation or application.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The sandy site is easy to dig and warms quickly, and its good drainage suits vegetables, but it holds little water and few nutrients, so it needs watering often and regular manure. Because the borehole is close, frequent watering is practical, and manure, compost and mulch would steadily improve the soil. The clay site holds water and nutrients well, but it is heavy to dig, may become waterlogged in the rains, and in the dry season the pupils would have to carry water 400 m. On balance the sandy site is better: its weaknesses can be managed, while the clay site's lack of water cannot.

explanation: Good answers weigh soil properties against practical factors and reach a justified decision.
hints: Weigh the soil properties against the practical problem of water supply.
Say how each site's weaknesses could be reduced.
